quizzes.title: Checkpoint 1 — Hierarchy, Layout, and Clarity
quizzes.intro: Check foundational visual and usability principles before forms, patterns, and critique practice.

questions.prompt: What is the primary aesthetic goal emphasized for UI?

options.text: Trendiness even if tasks are confusing
Clarity so users know what things are and what to do next
Maximum decoration on every pixel
Hiding all actions as a puzzle

questions.explanation: Professionals chase clarity; beauty that blocks tasks fails.

wrongExplanations.d: Invisible interactivity is a failure mode.

options.text: By making everything equally bold
Through size, weight, contrast, color, position, and spacing differences
Only by adding more icons
By removing the page title always

questions.explanation: Hierarchy orders attention; equal competition creates noise.

wrongExplanations.a: If everything is bold, nothing is.
wrongExplanations.c: Icons alone do not create structure.
wrongExplanations.d: Titles often support wayfinding and hierarchy.

questions.prompt: What does proximity help with in layout?

options.text: Grouping related items together
Scattering related controls randomly
Encoding meaning by color alone
Removing alignment on purpose

questions.explanation: Related elements should sit together; space separates unrelated groups.

options.text: Pale-on-pale text always looks more professional in real conditions
Readable contrast helps users perceive text and essential controls, including in tough viewing conditions
Contrast only matters for print posters
Low contrast improves outdoor readability

questions.explanation: Low contrast is a common beginner failure that harms usability and accessibility.

wrongExplanations.a: Soft low contrast often fails in practice.

options.text: Cues that communicate possible actions, like pressable-looking buttons
Secret features with no visible cues
Only backend database keys
Decorative gradients with no meaning

questions.explanation: Signifiers help users discover affordances without hunting.

wrongExplanations.c: That is not a UI principle term here.
wrongExplanations.d: Decoration without meaning does not signify action.

quizzes.title: Checkpoint 2 — Feedback, Forms, and Consistency
quizzes.intro: Test system status, errors, patterns, and interaction quality.

questions.prompt: Why does feedback matter after actions?

options.text: Silent interfaces make users repeat clicks or abandon tasks
Users never need to know if a payment failed
Every tiny save needs fireworks
Feedback should only be color with no text

questions.explanation: Timely, proportionate feedback communicates system status.

wrongExplanations.b: Failures especially need clear next steps.

options.text: “Invalid input”
“Enter a date like 2026-03-30”
No message at all
Blame the user with sarcasm

questions.explanation: Blame-free guidance that explains how to fix the problem aids recovery.

questions.prompt: What does consistency across screens primarily reduce?

options.text: Learning cost for similar actions
The need for any hierarchy
The need for labels
Accessibility requirements

questions.explanation: Reusable patterns help users transfer knowledge.

questions.prompt: What is a common forms mistake?

options.text: Visible labels and helpful validation
Placeholder-only labels and rude late errors
Asking only for needed fields
Grouping related fields

questions.explanation: Placeholder-only labels and poor validation hurt completion.

questions.prompt: How should primary actions be treated?

options.text: Visually dominant and verb-led, without five equal competitors
Identical in weight to every other button
Hidden behind icon-only mystery controls always
Named “Submit” regardless of context

questions.explanation: One clear primary CTA reduces choice paralysis.

quizzes.title: Final Quiz — Critique, Accessibility, and Judgment
quizzes.intro: Use the full lesson. Focus on accessibility, ethics, content realism, and professional critique.

questions.prompt: Why design with realistic content instead of only lorem ipsum?

options.text: Because edge lengths, errors, and empty states reveal whether layouts are honest
Because fake text always proves usability
Because content never affects UI
Because long names never appear in products

questions.explanation: Content-first design exposes fragile layouts early.

options.text: “I don’t like it.”
“The primary CTA competes with three equal buttons, so hierarchy is unclear.”
“Make it pop” with no principle
“Add more gradients” as the only note

wrongExplanations.c: Vague directives do not teach fixes.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes dark patterns from honest persuasion?

options.text: Dark patterns trick or hide exits; honest persuasion can highlight a plan without deception
Any recommended plan is a dark pattern
Dark patterns always increase long-term trust
Ethics do not apply to UI

questions.explanation: Professionals avoid manipulative patterns that destroy trust.

wrongExplanations.c: Dark patterns erode trust and invite churn.
wrongExplanations.d: Attention ethics are part of craft.

options.text: Color as the only status signal
Readable contrast, visible labels, and visible keyboard focus
Placeholder-only forms for a cleaner look
Tiny touch targets to save space

questions.explanation: Accessibility basics are quality requirements, not optional polish.

questions.prompt: What should component specs include beyond the happy path?

options.text: Only the default pretty state
States such as loading, error, disabled, focus, and empty where relevant
No behavior notes for developers
A single screenshot with no edge cases

questions.explanation: Incomplete states become inconsistent implementations and user confusion.

wrongExplanations.c: Behavior specs matter for engineering handoff.

questions.prompt: Which standard captures the course’s end goal?

options.text: Design so a busy stranger can understand state and act without a guided tour
Prioritize decoration over task success
Copy trends without annotating principles
Treat this as only a Figma click tutorial

questions.explanation: Principles-focused clarity is the course standard—not tool training.

wrongExplanations.d: This course is explicitly not a Figma tutorial.
